text: A single pass or fail at the end hides where things went wrong. A retrieval augmented answer depends on a search and then on the writing that uses its results, and an agent's answer sits at the end of a chain of tool calls. To improve such systems you need to measure each stage, so that a failure points at its cause rather than merely at the output.

For retrieval pipelines, split the evaluation in two. Score the retrieval stage with recall and nDCG against labelled passages, exactly as in the hybrid search lesson. Then score the answer for faithfulness, meaning every claim is supported by the retrieved text, and for correctness. Read together they diagnose the failure: if the right passage was retrieved but the answer is wrong, fix the generation, and if it was never retrieved, no prompt will rescue the answer.

For agents, judge the outcome by checking the state of the world rather than the agent's own report. An agent that says it fixed the bug may not have, so run the test suite. An agent that says it booked the meeting may have booked the wrong day, so query the calendar. Checks written in code against the final state are the most trustworthy grader an agent eval can have.

The path matters too. A trajectory check reads the sequence of tool calls and asks whether the agent used appropriate tools, passed valid arguments, avoided forbidden actions, and finished within a sensible number of steps. An agent can reach the right outcome by a dangerous or wasteful route, and trajectory checks catch that even when the final state looks perfect.

Agents are also stochastic, so run every task several times. The measure pass at k, from the lesson on evaluating models, asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeds, which suits settings where you can try repeatedly and keep a success. A user relying on an assistant needs the opposite: success every time. The tau bench study measured this as pass hat k, the chance that all k attempts succeed, which for independent attempts is roughly p to the power k, so even ninety percent per attempt falls below sixty percent over five attempts.

In practice the pieces form a cycle. An offline suite of tasks runs on every change to the prompt, the tools or the model, just as unit tests run on every change to code. In production, a sample of real traces is graded continuously by a validated judge, failures are read and categorised, and the worst of them are added to the offline suite, so each mistake is caught at most once in front of users.

That completes the applied layer: retrieval you can measure and tune, a harness that makes each call dependable, agents with budgets and memory, and evaluations that tell you whether a change truly helped. Underneath all of it is the next token predictor you have spent this course building. Next come the capstones, beginning with a digit recogniser built from scratch in NumPy.
